analysis.one_liner: Creates a national Medicare-style health plan covering all Americans, phased in from 2026.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on December 21, 2022, with 5 Democratic cosponsors, referred to six committees, and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new national health insurance program run by the Department of Health and Human Services that covers everyone living in the United States, starting in 2026. It would pay for doctor visits, hospital care, prescription drugs, dental, hearing, vision, and long-term care at home, with no deductibles and premiums capped at 8% of income. People with employer or other coverage could keep it temporarily, and private insurers could only sell plans that add benefits on top of the new program. To pay for it, the bill would raise taxes on the wealthy, corporations, tobacco, alcohol, and sugary drinks, and let the government negotiate or license drug patents when prices are too high.
analysis.who_benefits: Every US resident who has no comprehensive coverage, everyone currently paying Medicare or private-insurance premiums and deductibles, people with disabilities waiting for Medicare, and families needing long-term care. Low- and middle-income households pay no or reduced premiums and face annual out-of-pocket caps of $3,500 per person or $5,000 per household, with $0 for people under 200% of the poverty line.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a national health insurance program covering all US residents by 2026, including dental, hearing, vision, and home- and community-based long-term care.
Eliminates deductibles and caps annual out-of-pocket costs at $3,500 per person or $5,000 per household, with zero cost-sharing for households under 200% of the poverty line.
Caps premiums at 8% of income and provides full subsidies for households under 200% of poverty; employers may shift employees into the program instead of offering coverage.
Bars private insurers from selling duplicative coverage, effectively moving employer and individual market insurance into the public program over a transition period.
Funds the program by sunsetting the 2017 tax law and adding surtaxes, Medicare payroll and investment-income taxes, tobacco, alcohol, and sugary-drink excise taxes.

analysis.who_pays: High-income households and corporations (surtax, higher payroll and investment-income taxes, end of the 2017 tax cuts), tobacco, alcohol, and sugary-drink consumers, private health insurers (no more duplicative coverage), and brand-name drug makers, which would face negotiated prices and possible forced patent licensing if they refuse.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners, corporations, insurers, drug makers

drawbacks.text: The tax base is large and novel; independent cost estimates are unavailable because the bill never received a Congressional Budget Office score, so financing adequacy is untested.

The program phases in over nearly a decade (exchanges sunset in 2030, Medicaid transitions in 2032), creating a long, complicated transition that could leave some people without coverage if implementation slips.

Reimbursement is set near existing Medicare/Medicaid rates with hospital floors; hospitals and providers could see lower payments than from private insurance, which critics say could reduce access in some areas.

Even supporters of universal coverage differed on the design: it keeps private Medicare Advantage-style plans (renamed 'Medicare Advantage for America') and leaves employer coverage as a qualified opt-out for many years, so it is not a single-payer bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households, the benefit is straightforward: everyone gets coverage, deductibles disappear, and premium and out-of-pocket costs are capped by income. The costs are real but diffuse: higher taxes on high earners, corporations, and consumers of taxed products, and lower payment rates for hospitals and drug makers. The biggest uncertainty is the long transition — the bill tries to move everyone onto one program over six years while keeping private plans as a bridge, which is harder to administer than either a quick switch or the status quo.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the final two weeks of the 117th Congress and referred to six committees; none acted before the Congress ended January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Representative Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on December 21, 2022, with five Democratic cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Judiciary, Natural Resources, Education and Labor, and House Administration committees.
No committee reported the bill, no hearing is recorded, and no floor vote ever occurred; all actions lapse with the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.
The text and short title ('Medicare for America Act of 2019') match an earlier Medicare for America proposal first circulated in 2019, reintroduced here in the final days of a Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers, large employers that fund coverage, hospitals paid above Medicare rates by private insurers, and brand-name drug makers all keep the status quo, since the bill never advanced. High-income households and corporations also keep the 2017 tax cuts the bill would have sunsetted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, drug makers, and high earners

industries.note: The bill bans selling coverage duplicating the public program, shrinking insurers to supplemental and Medicare Advantage-style plans, with broker fees banned. Insurers' core individual and employer market revenue would migrate to the public program.
The government would negotiate drug prices and could issue competitive licenses to manufacture drugs whose prices it deems excessive. Direct-to-consumer drug advertising would be temporarily banned.

Payment would be tied to Medicare/Medicaid rates with a 110% hospital floor — lower than typical private-insurer rates but guaranteed, and with federal payments covering the Medicaid rate difference through 2030.
The bill preserves a Medicare Advantage-style private option (at 95% of public-plan costs) but repeals MA bonus payments and restricts mid-year provider removals.

Large employers could eventually shift workers into the public program instead of paying for coverage, but small employers would have to either provide qualifying coverage or enroll employees. The repeal of the high-cost 'Cadillac' excise tax helps employers with richer plans.
Higher excise taxes on cigarettes, small cigars, alcohol, and sugared drinks would fund the program; these taxes raise costs for consumers of those products too.
The bill sunsets the 2017 tax law (Public Law 115-97), adds a surtax, expands Medicare payroll and net investment income taxes, and ends health savings account deductions.
